beats.say: Here's demo-presentation in seven steps, from install to a reviewed video. Your machine needs only uv and git.
Step one: install it. In Claude Code it's a plugin. Other agents use npx skills, or unzip the release.
You end up with this folder: the skill file, its command line, and the scene renderers.
Step two: give your project a .demo folder. Its config.toml sets the theme, the voice, and a lexicon for words the voice gets wrong.
A web app also sets a base URL, and the services to start before recording.
brief.md tells the agent what it may show, and what never goes on camera. Keep the runs folder out of git; videos don't belong in the repo.
Step three: ask your agent for a video, in plain words.

do.user: make a demo video of the new settings page

beats.say: It reads your brief and says what it will do. Ask for an outline first if you want to approve a plan.

do.agent: I'll read `.demo/brief.md`, write a script, check a storyboard frame by frame, then record it.

prepare.user: make a demo video of the new settings page

agent.text: I'll read `.demo/brief.md`, write a script, check a storyboard frame by frame, then record it.

beats.say: Step four is the agent's job. It creates a run, writes the script, and validates it.
Then it renders a storyboard, one frame per beat, and checks every frame itself before it records.
Only then does it build: narrate, record in real time, and stitch the video. And it sends you the link.
Remember the settings page you asked for? This is the kind of UI scene the agent records, here on the sample app.

chapter.title: Your app
chapter.description: a UI scene on the sample app

beats.say: It drives a real browser, clicks through to settings like a person would, and spotlights what the narration is about.
It turns on the weekly digest, and waits until the app says it saved.
And it types into the page, just as you would.
UI scenes aren't limited to your machine. A scene can open any site, like this project's page on GitHub.
For a site behind a login, the token comes from an environment variable, never from the script.
Step five: review it in the browser. The agent gives you a link from demo url, a page on your own machine.
It opens on the video, with a live transcript underneath. Press space to play.
Click any word in the transcript to jump to it, and use the arrow keys to step through.
To comment, pause where something should change and press C. The comment is pinned to that moment.
Write what you want changed.
Press Mark region, and drag over the part of the frame you mean.
Then add it. It joins the list on the right, and a pin marks it on the timeline.
If the voice says a word wrong, pause and click that word.
Press Edit pronunciation, write how it should sound, and press Listen to check it.
Save puts it in the project's pronunciation library, so every video says it that way.
The Script and storyboard tab shows every beat with its frame. You can edit the narration right here.
Or press Request change on a scene or a beat, and say what you want.

fill.text: Say the file name out loud.

beats.say: Change requests collects them all in one place for the agent.
Re-render changes runs the same commands the agent would, for only what changed.
When it's right, press Approve video. If not, tell your agent you left feedback, or paste it the prompt from Copy agent prompt.
Then tell your agent you left feedback. It reads every comment with demo review, mapped to its beat.

do.user: I left comments on the video

beats.say: It edits the script, re-renders only what changed, replies to each comment, and sends the link again.

do.agent: Made the arrow label bigger, said the file name out loud, and added the version. Same link as before.

beats.say: Step six is optional: add a publish command to config.toml, and demo publish sends the video wherever your team keeps them.
Step seven, when something goes wrong: start with demo doctor. It shows what's installed and what will install on first use.

beats.say: If screenshots fail, add the software GL flag. If a UI scene times out, storyboard it headed to watch the browser.
That's it: install, set up .demo, ask, let the agent build, review, and publish if you want to.
